workEn: The Secret History of the Mongols
title: 元朝秘史 §§253–253
titleEn: The Secret History of the Mongols — §253: The Altan Qan Submits, and Qasar Takes Beijing
part: §253 — The Altan Qan Submits, and Qasar Takes Beijing
source: Mongγol-un niγuča tobčiyan (The Secret History of the Mongols), §§253–253, in the Ming Chinese-character phonetic transcription, as edited with a romanized reading by Shiratori Kurakichi 白鳥庫吉, 音訳蒙文元朝秘史 (Tokyo, 1943), itself based on the Ye Dehui 葉德輝 printed edition of 1905/1908; text taken from the Japanese Wikisource transcription, archived and verified against it character for character. Shiratori died in 1942, so the edition was public domain in Japan before the URAA date and was never restored in the United States. Section numbering (§) is the standard citation system. Romanization convention: Shiratori's, kept exactly as he prints it (γ, ġ, ṅ, ž, č, and the raised dot of γ̇). Translations are made fresh from the Mongolian, with the Ming interlinear Chinese glosses as the primary crib. No modern translation was consulted. langCode is null: there is no text-to-speech for Middle Mongol.
about: The Altan Qan, in Nanjing, submits and sends his son to serve as Chinggis's guard (§253). Chinggis withdraws by the Chabchiyal Pass and sends Qasar with the troops of the left hand along the sea, with orders to take Beijing, deal with the Jurchen Buqanu, and then come together again at the great camp. Grammar to watch: the long converb chains in -žu/-žü; the causatives in -ġül-/-γ̇ul-; the reflexive -(i)jen; the plural polite imperative -dqun/-dkün (Ming 您); and the Ming glossators' Chinese place names (Nanjing, the Juyong Pass, Daning).
draftNote: The Mongol readings follow Shiratori throughout; the English is a first drafting.

sentences.t: Altan Qān Nangiṅ orožu öġer(i)-jen elsen mürügüžü

morph.gloss: Altan, gold; here the title of the Jin emperor (Altan Qaγan), a name and title [金]
ruler, sovereign, khan (title; the short form after a name) [皇帝]
Nanjing (Han 南京), the Jin southern capital, Kaifeng (Ming 汴梁) [汴梁]
own, self (the (i) is Shiratori's linking vowel) [自己(自的行)]
to submit (stem inferred from the Ming) [歸附]
to bow, strike the head to the ground (stem inferred; Ming 叩頭) [叩頭着]

sentences.l: Altan Qan, Nanjing entering, own submitting, bowing,
sentences.i: The Altan Qan entered Nanjing, submitted of his own accord, bowed to the ground,
sentences.n: The unit is the opening of a converb chain whose verb comes in the next unit (iležüġü, ‘sent’): orožu (oro- ‘enter’ + converb -žu; Ming 入着), öġer(i)-jen elsen (öġer ‘own, self’ + the reflexive -(i)jen, Ming 自己 自的行; else- ‘submit’ + converb -n, Ming 歸附), mürügüžü (stem mürügü- inferred from Ming 叩頭 ‘kowtow’, + converb -žü). Altan Qān is the Jin emperor (Ming 金 皇帝) and is not named further. Nangiṅ is Han 南京 ‘southern capital’, which the Ming glosses 汴梁 (Kaifeng); I write ‘Nanjing’ as in §§249–252.

sentences.t: Teṅgeri neretü köġü-ben žaγ̇un nöködtü-ji Čiṅgis Qaγan-dur turγaγ boltuγai keġen iležüġü.

morph.gloss: Tenggeri, Heaven; here a man's name (Ming 人名) [人名]
son (short form of köġün) [兒子自的行]
reflexive-possessive: one's own (front-vowel form, after the front-vowel stem köġü)
Chinggis (Shiratori's spelling), a man's name [太祖︀]
optative: let it be, let him be (third person, back-vowel form)
past narrative (Ming 來了; the ending -žüġü is read from the Ming only; uncertain)

sentences.l: Tenggeri named son-his-own, hundred companion-having-(object), Chinggis Qaγan-to guard let-be saying, sent.
sentences.i: He sent his own son, named Tenggeri, with a hundred companions, saying, “Let him be a guard to Chinggis Qahan.”
sentences.n: Read as: [object] … keġen iležüġü, ‘sent [the object], saying “…”’. The object is the Altan Qan’s own son (köġü-ben: ‘son’ + reflexive -ben, which points back to the Altan Qan), named Teṅgeri (neretü: nere ‘name’ + -tü ‘having’, Ming 名字有的; Teṅgeri is a man’s name here, Ming 人名), and žaγ̇un nöködtü-ji, ‘the hundred-companion-having’, -ji marking the object (Ming 行). I take the hundred companions as the son’s retinue; whether they are a second object or a description of the son is not settled, and ‘with a hundred companions’ fits both. The speech is only Čiṅgis Qaγan-dur turγaγ boltuγai, ‘let (him) be a guard to Chinggis Qahan’ (bol- ‘be’ + optative -tuγai, Ming 做者; turγaγ, Ming 侍衞 ‘guard’), closed by keġen (keġe- ‘say’ + -n, Ming 麽道). iležüġü (Ming 敎來了) is ile- ‘send’ with an ending -žüġü that I can read as past only from the Ming. Shiratori marks no quotation here; the marks in `i` are mine.

sentences.t: Ima-da elsegdežü Čiṅgis Qaγan ičuja keġen

morph.gloss: he, that one (a pronoun stem, Ming 他) [他 行]
dative-locative: to, at (back-vowel form); with the passive verb, probably the agent, ‘by him’
Chinggis (Shiratori's spelling), a man's name [太祖︀]
to withdraw, retreat (stem inferred from the Ming 退) [退咱]
linking -u- + hortative -ja: let us … (Ming 咱; uncertain)

sentences.l: Him-by being-submitted-to, Chinggis Qaγan let-us-withdraw saying,
sentences.i: Having been submitted to by him, Chinggis Qahan said, “Let us withdraw.”
sentences.n: Ima-da is the pronoun ima ‘he’ + -da (Ming 他 行). With the passive verb it is read as the one by whom: elsegdežü is else- ‘submit’ + passive -gde- + converb -žü (Ming 被歸附着, ‘being submitted to’), so Chinggis is the one submitted to, by the Altan Qan. Ming 他 行 would also fit plain ‘to him’, but then the passive has no agent; the reading is not certain. ičuja is ič- ‘withdraw’ (stem inferred from Ming 退) + a linking -u- + hortative -ja (Ming 咱, ‘let us’); the ending is uncertain. keġen closes this short speech. Shiratori marks no quotation; the marks in `i` are mine.

sentences.t: Čabčijal(i)-jar tende ičurun Qasar-i žeġün γar-un čeriġüd(i)-jer dalai kižin ilerün

words.reading: 察卜赤牙里-牙舌兒 Čabčijal(i)-jar

morph.gloss: Chabchiyal, the Juyong Pass (Ming 居庸關) [居庸關 依着]
to withdraw (stem inferred from the Ming 退) [退時]
Qasar, a man's name (Chinggis's brother) [人名 行]

words.reading: 扯舌里兀的-耶舌兒 čeriġüd(i)-jer

morph.gloss: instrumental: with, by means of (the (i) is Shiratori's) [敎]
along the edge of, following the shore (Ming 㳂) [㳂]
converb of time: when, as …ing (front-vowel form; Ming 時)

sentences.l: Chabchiyal-by there withdrawing, Qasar-(object) left hand’s troops-with sea along sending,
sentences.i: As he withdrew there by way of the Chabchiyal Pass, sending Qasar along the sea with the troops of the left hand,
sentences.n: This is narrative, not speech: ičurun (Ming 退時) is ič- ‘withdraw’ + -urun ‘when, as …ing’, and ilerün (Ming 去時) is ile- ‘send’ + -rün, ‘when sending’ (the Ming 去 ‘go’ would give ‘going’, a possible alternative). Čabčijal(i)-jar is the Juyong Pass (Ming 居庸關 依着) with the instrumental -(i)jar, ‘by way of’; Qasar-i is accusative, the one sent. žeġün γar-un čeriġüd(i)-jer is ‘with the troops of the left hand’ (čerig + plural -üd + instrumental -(i)jer; Ming 左 手的 軍每敎), presumably the left wing of the army. kižin (Ming 㳂) ‘along’ the sea. The clause leads straight into the orders of the next unit.

morph.gloss: Beijing (Han 北京 ‘northern capital’); the Ming glosses 大寗 Daning, so probably not today’s Beijing [大寗]
to descend, come down (Ming 下; of a city, to bring it down, take it) [下您]
plural polite imperative: do (you all) (Ming 您)

sentences.n: The orders to Qasar begin here, in the plural polite imperative -dqun (baγu- + -dqun; Ming 下您, where 您 marks the polite ‘you’, as in iredkün below). baγu- is ‘come down, descend’ and, said of a city, Ming 下: ‘bring it down’, take it; balaγasu has lost its n in print. Bēgiṅ is Han 北京 ‘northern capital’, but the Ming glosses it 大寗, Daning, so it is probably not today’s Beijing; I write ‘Beijing’ only because the Han does. Shiratori marks no opening quotation; his one closing mark comes at iredkün in unit 9, so I open the speech at the first imperative (the mark is mine, in `i` only). An earlier opening, at ičuja or at Qasar-i, is possible; I chose here because ičuja keġen already closes its own short speech and ilerün is a plain narrative converb. The reading is uncertain.

sentences.t: Bēgiṅ balaγasan-i elšeġülžü činana Žürčed-ün Buqanu-ji daγ̇arin odču

morph.gloss: Beijing (Han 北京); the Ming glosses 大寗 Daning [大寗]
on that side, beyond (adverb, Ming 那廂) [那廂]
to pass through, go by (Ming 經過) [經過]

sentences.l: Beijing city-(object) submission-causing, beyond Jurchen’s Buqanu-(object) passing going,
sentences.i: make the city of Beijing submit, then go on beyond it, passing Buqanu of the Jurchen,
sentences.n: A chain of orders. elšeġülžü is else- ‘submit’ + causative -ġül- + -žü (Ming 敎歸附着, ‘having made submit’; Shiratori prints elše-). činana (Ming 那廂) is ‘on that side, beyond’. Žürčed-ün Buqanu-ji is ‘Buqanu of the Jurchen’ (Žürčed + genitive -ün; Ming 女眞的 人名行), with the accusative -ji. daγ̇arin odču (Ming 經過 去着) is ‘passing, going’. balaγasan-i is printed with a for u (accusative -i).

morph.gloss: to hunt down, seize (stem inferred from the Ming 勦捕) [勦捕您]
plural polite imperative: do (you all) (Ming 您)

sentences.i: if Buqanu thinks of rebellion, hunt him down; if he submits,
sentences.n: Two conditions with opposite orders. sedkiġesü is sedki- ‘think’ + conditional -ġesü (Ming 想呵, ‘if he thinks’); bulγa (Ming 反) is ‘rebellion’. qaγ̇uludqun is qaγ̇ulu- (stem inferred from Ming 勦捕, ‘hunt down, seize’) + the plural polite imperative -dqun (Ming 您), as in baγudqun. elseġesü is else- + -ġesü (Ming 歸附呵, ‘if he submits’). What follows for the second condition is in the next unit.

sentences.t: in-ü kižiγ̇ar balaγad an-u daγ̇arin Ula, Naγ̇u müred kižin odču

morph.gloss: his, her, its (third-person genitive; here set before its noun, in-ü kižiγ̇ar) [他的]
their (back-vowel companion of in-ü, third-person genitive) [他的]
to pass through, go by [經過]
Na’u (Shiratori’s Naγ̇u), a river name [河名]
along the edge of, following (Ming 㳂) [㳂]

sentences.l: his border cities their passing, Ula, Na’u rivers along going,
sentences.i: pass through his border cities and go along the rivers Ula and Na’u,
sentences.n: The orders go on: ‘pass through his border cities and go along the rivers’. in-ü and an-u both have the Ming 他的; the glossary reads in-ü as ‘his’ and an-u as ‘their’, each placed after its noun. Here in-ü stands before kižiγ̇ar, so I read in-ü kižiγ̇ar balaγad as ‘his border cities’ and an-u, after balaγad, as ‘their’ pointing back at the cities; whether the two are meant separately is not clear. kižiγ̇ar (Ming 邊) is ‘edge, border’; balaγad is the plural of balaγasun; daγ̇arin is ‘passing’ (Ming 經過). Ula and Na’u are river names (Ming 河名 each); müred is müren ‘river’ + plural -d (Ming 河每); kižin (Ming 㳂) ‘along’. Na’u is Shiratori’s Naγ̇u, written with an apostrophe for γ̇ as in other names.

sentences.t: Taγ̇ur müren öġede dabažu jeke aγ̇uruγ-tur neilen iredkün" keġežü

morph.gloss: Ta’ur (Shiratori’s Taγ̇ur), a river name [河名]
against, facing, upstream (Ming 逆着) [逆着]
to cross over, pass over [越着]

words.reading: 阿兀舌魯黑-圖舌兒 aγ̇uruγ-tur

morph.gloss: to join together, meet (Ming 相合) [相合]
plural polite imperative: do (you all) (Ming 您)

sentences.l: Ta’ur river against crossing, great camp-at joining come-ye saying,
sentences.i: cross the Ta’ur river against its flow, and come together at the great camp,” he said.
sentences.n: The speech ends here: iredkün” carries Shiratori’s only quotation mark, and keġežü (keġe- ‘say’ + -žü, Ming 說着) is ‘having said’. iredkün is ire- ‘come’ + the plural polite imperative -dkün, ‘come (you all)’ (Ming 來您), the same ending as -dqun. öġede (Ming 逆着) is ‘against’; whether that means upstream, or crossing in the teeth of the current, the Ming does not say, so `i` says ‘against its flow’. dabažu is daba- ‘cross’ + -žu (Ming 越着). aγ̇uruγ-tur is ‘at the camp’ (Ming 營盤 裏); neilen (Ming 相合) ‘joining, together’.

irebe is ire- ‘come’ + past -be (Ming 來了), ‘came’. It is a unit of its own because Shiratori’s full stop falls here, closing a sentence that began in unit 6, and the verb needs its own line after the speech. The subject is not stated; I take it to be Chinggis, the subject of the sentence so far, who has just given the orders. The Ming gives only 來了.

sentences.t: Qasar-luγ̇a nojad-ača Žürčedei, Alči, Tolun čerbi γurban-i ileldübe.

morph.gloss: Qasar, a man's name [人名 一同]
cherbi, an office (Ming 官名) [官名]

sentences.l: Qasar-with officers-from Jürchedei, Alchi, Tolun cherbi, three-(object) sent-together.
sentences.i: With Qasar he sent along three of the officers, Jürchedei, Alchi and Tolun the cherbi.
sentences.n: A new sentence. Qasar-luγ̇a is Qasar + comitative -luγ̇a, ‘with Qasar’ (Ming 一同). nojad-ača is noyan ‘officer’ + plural -d + ablative -ača, ‘from among the officers’ (Ming 官人每行). Then three names and čerbi (Ming 官名, an office whose meaning is not known; see §224), then γurban-i, ‘the three’ + -i. I take čerbi as Tolun’s title only; it stands directly before the numeral, so it could equally be the title of all three, and I leave that open. ileldübe is ile- ‘send’ + -ldü- ‘together’ + past -be (Ming 敎共去了).

sentences.t: Qasar Bēgiṅ balaγasun oroγ̇ulžu Žürčed-ün Buqanu-ji elseġülžü mör-e bümüi balaγasan-i oroγ̇uluγ̇ad

morph.gloss: Beijing (Han 北京); the Ming glosses 大寗 Daning [大寗]

sentences.l: Qasar Beijing city entering-causing, Jurchen’s Buqanu-(object) submission-causing, road-on being city-(object) entering-causing,
sentences.i: Qasar made the city of Beijing surrender, made Buqanu of the Jurchen submit, and made the cities that lay on the road surrender,
sentences.n: Three causative clauses with Qasar as subject; their finite verb is irebe in the next unit. oroγ̇ulžu is oro- ‘enter’ + causative -γ̇ul- + -žu (Ming 敎投降着, ‘made surrender’); elseġülžü is as in unit 6 (Ming 敎歸附着). mör-e bümüi balaγasan-i is ‘the cities that are on the road’ (mör ‘road’ + -e ‘on’; bü- ‘be’ + -mui; Ming 路行 有的 城子行), accusative -i, with balaγasan printed for balaγasun. oroγ̇uluγ̇ad is the same causative with converb -γ̇ad (Ming 敎投入了).

sentences.t: Qasar Taγ̇ur müren öġede irežü jeke aγ̇uruγ-tur baγ̇užu irebe.

morph.gloss: Ta’ur (Shiratori’s Taγ̇ur), a river name [河名]

words.reading: 阿兀舌魯黑-圖舌兒 aγ̇uruγ-tur

sentences.l: Qasar Ta’ur river against coming, great camp-at descending, came.
sentences.i: Qasar came against the flow of the Ta’ur river, alighted at the great camp, and arrived.
sentences.n: Qasar’s return, the order of unit 9 carried out: Taγ̇ur müren öġede irežü (Ming 逆着 來着) is ‘coming against the Ta’ur river’, jeke aγ̇uruγ-tur is ‘at the great camp’ (Ming 營盤 裏), baγ̇užu (Ming 下着) is baγu- ‘descend’, here ‘alight, make camp’, and irebe closes the sentence begun in unit 12.
